summary: Reserves three IPv4 unicast address blocks for use in examples in specifications and other documents, so examples do not collide with real networks. The blocks are 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, and 203.0.113.0/24. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you write a pretend address in a textbook, you should not use someone's real one. These three ranges are set aside for pretend examples.

questions: which ipv4 addresses are for documentation
can i use 203.0.113.0/24 on the internet
subtitle: Three IPv4 address blocks set aside so examples in documents never collide with real networks.

tldr.problem: Documents and specifications need example IPv4 addresses, but using real ones risks conflict and confusion with addresses assigned for other purposes.
tldr.mechanism: Three blocks are reserved for documentation: 192.0.2.0/24 (TEST-NET-1), 198.51.100.0/24 (TEST-NET-2) and 203.0.113.0/24 (TEST-NET-3).
tldr.outcome: These addresses SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet, and operators SHOULD treat them as non-routable and add them to packet filters. The RFC updates RFC 1166.

today: RFC 5737 is an Informational document from January 2010 that updates RFC 1166, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Reserve Example Addresses
sections.content:
Using designated ranges for documentation and examples reduces the chance of conflicts and confusion from using addresses assigned for something else. RFC 1166 had already reserved the first block, 192.0.2.0/24. The other two were recently allocated, mainly to make it easier to write examples that involve addresses from several networks.

Other documentation ranges already exist: the IPv6 documentation prefix (RFC 3849) and example domain names (RFC 2606). Documentation also uses the ranges reserved in RFC 1918.
sections.eli5: Textbook writers need pretend addresses, like using "Anytown" instead of a real town. These blocks are the pretend towns.

sections.title: The Three Blocks
sections.content: The RFC names three blocks, all /24 prefixes: 192.0.2.0/24 (TEST-NET-1), 198.51.100.0/24 (TEST-NET-2) and 203.0.113.0/24 (TEST-NET-3). IANA has recorded the allocation of all three in the IPv4 address registry, and no end party is to be assigned these addresses. The authors thank APNIC, which nominated the second and third blocks.
sections.eli5: There are three pretend neighborhoods, and nobody is allowed to really live in them.

sections.title: Operational Rules and 128.66.0.0/16
sections.content:
Addresses in the TEST-NET blocks SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet, and they are used without coordination with IANA or an Internet registry. Network operators SHOULD add the blocks to their list of non-routable address space and to packet filters if they are deployed. The blocks are not for local use, and the filters may be used in both local and public contexts.

The RFC also notes that 128.66.0.0/16 has been used in past examples. It was not in the list of special prefixes in RFC 3330 or its successors, so it is not reserved and can be used for regular address assignments with caution. The RFC says it has no security implications.
sections.eli5: Real networks should not carry mail to these pretend addresses, so routers are told to block them. The old pretend range 128.66.0.0/16 is not protected and may belong to a real person.
